newsitem.title: RWANDA: UN brings home Rwandans, military plans advance.
newsitem.headline: UN brings home Rwandans, military plans advance.

text.p: The U.N. agency UNHCR said on Friday its operation to bring home Rwandan refugees from Zaire was gaining pace, just as plans for a multinational military mission to find and help them began to fall into place.

The UNHCR spokesman in the Rwandan capital Kigali, Paul Stromberg, told Reuters that 1,000 Rwandans crossed the border south of Lake Kivu on Thursday to a transit area at Cyangugu near the Zairean town of Bukavu.

"It was the biggest single return in that area in a single day," he said. The agency is trucking another 700 refugees towards the border to the north of the lake on Friday, UNHCR officials in the Zairean town of Goma added.
"We've added 115 trucks to the fleet and 100 more are coming, for use in both Zaire and Rwanda," Stromberg said.
But aid agencies believe at least 200,000 Rwandan refugees, possibly up to 600,000, remain dispersed in eastern Zaire, short of food and in danger of attack by undisciplined militias.

The Rwandans, who fled to Zaire in 1994 after civil war and a rebel victory in their home country, abandoned their camps in October after fighting broke out between Zairean rebels, the Zairean army and Rwandan Hutu militias.
About 600,000 of them have now gone home but others, along with displaced Zaireans, are dispersed through the region.

Canada is coordinating plans to launch a rescue operation and after many false starts the signs now are that it will go ahead -- either in the form of airdrops of food or through ground troops to clear safe passages for aid agencies.

Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said in Tokyo on Friday that the Canadian commander of the proposed force, Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, had reached an understanding with the Zairean rebels, who control much of the border area.

"General Baril met with the commander of the force in that area (on Thursday), had some discussion with the combatants there and they have agreed to collaborate to make sure that there is no problem," Chretien said.
But it was not immediately clear that rebel leader Laurent Kabila had accepted the ground-troop option, which most aid agencies prefer and which the rebels have vigorously opposed.

The rebels, along with the Rwandan government, think that ground troops could strengthen the hand of ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, whose troops the rebels have routed. They argue that most Rwandan refugees have gone home anyway.

In an interview to be published on Monday in the Paris-based weekly Nouvel Afrique Asie, Kabila said his men would resist any French presence in a military force because of French intervention in support of Mobutu in the past.
"Let no one believe any longer that we'll keep our arms folded when we see the first French soldier or paratrooper in this region," he said.
The Canadians on the ground in central Africa continue to prefer deploying ground troops, with airdrops of food as a contingency option in case the first plan collapses.
A Canadian spokesman in Kigali said on Friday that the operation would take one step forward at the weekend when officers cross into Zaire on a reconnaissance mission.
The spokesman, Major Paul Dangerfield, said the team would include two or three officers going in with UNHCR personnel to find out where the refugees are.
"They will be unarmed and out of uniform and we expect them to go in on Saturday or Sunday," he told reporters.
In Ottawa on Thursday, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said that ambassadors from over 20 countries would meet on Friday to give the multinational operation final approval.

"We have now achieved an agreement," he said in a statement. The agreement is to set up a multinational headquarters in Uganda, pursue further reconnaissance and put in place a capability to carry out the airdrops.
Stromberg said some of the refugees reaching the Bukavu area were from a large concentration around the village of Numbi, where Baril estimates there are 150,000 to 200,000 refugees.
